versions.text:
When I was a child in Tessel Hollow, my grandfather rang the meetinghouse bell at noon. People liked to say it had come over the pass on an ox sled, and that his own father had helped haul it into the tower, but what I remember is the sound: a round, dark note that hummed for a full minute after the rope went slack.

The winter I turned twelve, that hum changed. Reverend Coombe was the first to say so, telling my grandfather after service that the bell rattled like a pan lid. My mother insisted afterward that she had heard it days earlier, and Miss Ardley, the schoolteacher, claimed the same, but it was the minister who climbed the tower with a lantern and found the crack.

At the town meeting in March, Mr. Pruett wanted to sell the bell to a collector in Brask and put the money toward the school roof, and someone else suggested setting it in the schoolyard. My grandfather said little. Afterward he took me up the tower and struck the bell once near the crack. The note came out split in two, a buzz laid over a groan.

"It used to answer itself," he said. "Now it only argues." Some neighbors valued the bell for its age, and a few for its value as a fire alarm, but he spoke about it the way a singer speaks about a voice. He argued that the metal should go to the foundry at Ludd and be poured again, and by summer the town had voted to send it. Keeping it ringing as it was, he said, would be like letting a choir sing flat forever.

The new bell came back in October, cast from the old one, and I was glad for him. Still, when I go home now and hear that bright, correct note, I find myself listening for the buzz underneath, the sound I grew up with, and missing it more than I can easily explain. Nell, my sister, laughs at me for it; she says the old bell sounded like a goat.

In Tessel Hollow my grandfather rang the meetinghouse bell, and he did it the same way every day of my childhood. At a quarter to twelve he left his workbench, climbed the forty-one steps, and pulled the rope nine times at noon exactly. People said the bell had a lovely voice, and that his father had hung it, but to him the job was simply a duty, like winding the clock.

The winter I turned twelve, my little sister Nell came home from sledding and announced that the bell sounded broken. Nobody believed her at first. Miss Ardley thought it was the cold that made it rattle, and Reverend Coombe blamed the wind in the louvers, but Nell kept on about it until my grandfather took a lantern up the tower and found the crack.

At the town meeting in March, some wanted to send the bell to the foundry at Ludd to be recast; Mr. Pruett wanted to sell it to a collector in Brask. Then, in the middle of the arguing, the Hask barn on the ridge caught fire. My grandfather ran to the tower and rang. I remember being struck by how far that wounded sound carried over the snow, and the volunteers came running from three farms away.

After that the question settled itself. A few people still talked about the bell's age, or about what the collector had offered, but my grandfather put the matter plainly at the next meeting: a bell that could bring men to a fire in four minutes was doing its work, cracked or whole. The town voted to leave it hanging and keep ringing it as it was. The schoolyard plan, which some of the mothers had liked, was quietly dropped.

It still hangs there. Visitors wince at noon, and the new minister once asked, very politely, whether something might be done about it. Nell rings it now when she is home, and every time it clanks out over the fields like a dropped kettle I find myself grinning. The town has a voice like a cracked plate, and it seems rather proud of it.

The year I turned twelve, Tessel Hollow was very nearly broke. The mill had closed, the school roof leaked into the reading corner, and the meetinghouse bell that my grandfather rang every noon was about the only thing in town worth much. Everyone knew its history, how it had come over the pass on an ox sled, but that winter people spoke mostly of what it might fetch.

It was Miss Ardley, the schoolteacher, who first heard the change. Walking her pupils home one January noon, she caught a rasp in the bell and sent a boy to tell my grandfather. My mother said later she had noticed it too, and Reverend Coombe agreed once it was pointed out, but Miss Ardley was the one who insisted someone climb up and look.

At the town meeting in March, some wanted to send the bell to the foundry at Ludd to be recast, and for a while the room was with them. Then my grandfather read out a letter from a collector in Brask who wanted old bells, cracked or whole, and named a figure larger than the cost of a new roof. Within a week a price had been struck, and the collector's men were measuring the tower door.

People were surprised, since he had rung it for forty years. Some had expected him to defend its age, or to ask that it be set in the schoolyard. But he had always talked about the bell the way he talked about a good cow or a sound roof, as something the town owned and could spend when it needed to. The roof, he said, was what mattered now. By April the bell was gone.

I was there when they lowered it. My grandfather watched with his hands in his pockets and said it was a fair trade. I suppose it was. Even so, I have sometimes wondered where the bell hangs now, or whether it sits in a warehouse with a paper tag on its lip, and the thought stays with me like a pebble in a shoe.

The meetinghouse bell in Tessel Hollow came over the pass on an ox sled in 1841, after the town had saved for it for eleven years. Near the top the sled broke an axle, and the men carried the bell the last mile on poles. My grandfather had rung it at noon for decades, and it had a deep, round voice, but the story of its arrival was what he told me most.

The winter I turned twelve, a Mr. Fenn came from the city to tune the meetinghouse organ. He was the first to hear it: at noon on his second day he frowned at the ceiling and asked my grandfather whether he knew his bell was cracked. Reverend Coombe had thought the new rasp was ice, and my mother had blamed the wind, but Mr. Fenn climbed the tower and showed us the crack.

At the town meeting in March, the warrant listed one proposal: send the bell to the foundry at Ludd to be recast. My grandfather rose and asked who in the room had carried it up the pass. Nobody had, but several had grandfathers who did. By the end of the evening the recasting article had been struck from the warrant, and Mr. Pruett's idea of selling to a collector in Brask got even fewer votes.

What the town did instead was my grandfather's idea. In May the bell was set on a stone base in the schoolyard, beside a plaque naming the men who had hauled it. A few people grumbled that it would have been more useful as a fire alarm, and some had wanted it rung cracked as before, but he said a bell that old belonged where children would ask about it. A smaller bell went up in the tower.

It is still there. Children climb on it and knock on its side to hear the dull clunk, and every fall the third grade learns about the ox sled. When I walk past, I put my hand on the cool green metal, and think that it ended up in exactly the right place. My sister says it looks lonely out there; I have never thought so.

My great-grandfather, Tobias Wren, was the man who hung the meetinghouse bell in Tessel Hollow. He rigged the beam himself, set the yoke, and rang it for thirty years before handing the rope to my grandfather, then a boy of fifteen. My grandfather spoke of him every noon, as if the bell's deep, round note were his father's voice still calling across the fields.

The winter I turned twelve, my mother was the first to hear the crack. She came in from hanging laundry saying the bell sounded hoarse. My sister thought she was imagining it, and the organ tuner who visited that month blamed the cold, but my mother walked my grandfather to the tower herself, and there it was.

At the town meeting in March, most people favored sending the bell to the foundry at Ludd to be recast, and Mr. Pruett spoke for selling it to a collector in Brask. My grandfather sat through both arguments with his hat on his knees. It was my mother who finally struck on the answer: if the town wanted a new bell it could have one, and the old bell could come home to the family that had hung it.

In May four neighbors helped us lay it on oak blocks in the back of our barn. Some people thought it a waste, since it might have stood in the schoolyard or raised money for the roof, and Reverend Coombe worried the town would miss its sound. My grandfather said only that he would rather sit with it than hear a stranger ring it, and most evenings he did, on an upturned crate, his hand resting on the yoke Tobias had set.

The barn is mine now, and the bell is still there under a canvas sheet. Some evenings I sit on the same crate and think about my mother standing up in that meeting, and about the neighbors who carried four hundred pounds of bronze across our yard for no pay, and I hope they knew what they gave him. My sister calls it the family's heaviest heirloom and laughs, but she visits it too.
